summary: Defines a two-way mapping for presence information, the is-this-person-available status, between SIP and XMPP. It was replaced by RFC 8048.

eli5.summary: If one chat system says a friend is online, this document explains how to tell the other chat system too. A newer version has replaced it.

questions: how to share presence between sip and xmpp
how do sip and xmpp handle presence differently
how do gateways map xmpp to sip
what happens when a sip subscription expires
subtitle: Sharing online status between two different instant messaging protocols

tldr.problem: The Internet has two major presence systems: SIP/SIMPLE for voice and multimedia communication, and XMPP/Jabber for instant messaging. When one system wants to know if someone in the other system is available, there was no standard way to translate that request.
tldr.mechanism: Defines bidirectional mappings between SIP and XMPP presence constructs. SIP subscription requests map to XMPP subscription stanzas, SIP NOTIFY messages map to XMPP presence updates, and special handling bridges the differences in how each protocol manages subscriptions (SIP subscriptions expire and refresh, while XMPP subscriptions are long-lived).
tldr.outcome: Gateways can now translate presence between the two protocols at the protocol level, enabling interworking. RFC 8048 later superseded this with enhancements.

facts.label: XMPP presence type values
facts.value: subscribe, subscribed, unsubscribe, unsubscribed, probe, unavailable

today: RFC 7248 is a Proposed Standard that was superseded by RFC 8048, which extends presence interworking to instant messaging. The presence mapping defined here remains foundational for SIP-XMPP gateways that enable cross-system interoperability.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
Two major presence technologies are widely deployed: SIP (Session Initiation Protocol) with its SIMPLE presence extensions, and XMPP (Extensible Messaging and Presence Protocol, descended from Jabber). Both let users ask whether a contact is online, but they use different protocols and have different semantics.

RFC 7247 (the predecessor to this document) defines architectural assumptions for SIP-XMPP interworking, including how to map addresses and handle errors. This document focuses specifically on presence: the ability to query and receive notifications about whether someone is available for communication.

Both protocols support basic presence (online or offline) and richer information like availability states (away, do not disturb). This RFC covers the basic case; extensions for richer presence are left to future documents.
sections.eli5: Two big instant messaging systems exist: SIP (used for phone calls) and XMPP (used for chat). This document explains how to make them understand each other's "I'm online" messages.

sections.title: Subscription Models and Core Concepts
sections.content:
SIP presence subscriptions are short-lived and managed with SUBSCRIBE requests. A client sends SUBSCRIBE specifying a default expiration time (usually 3600 seconds, or one hour). The server acknowledges with a 200 OK response and then sends NOTIFY messages carrying presence information. Before the subscription expires, the client must refresh it by sending another SUBSCRIBE.

XMPP presence subscriptions are long-lived. A user sends a subscribe request as an XMPP presence stanza of type "subscribe". The contact can accept (by returning type "subscribed") or decline (by returning type "unsubscribed"). Once accepted, the subscription persists until explicitly cancelled.

A key challenge: SIP expects subscriptions to time out and be refreshed, while XMPP expects them to remain until actively cancelled. Gateways must bridge this difference. When an XMPP user wants to subscribe to a SIP user, the gateway must periodically refresh the SIP subscription to keep it alive. Conversely, when a SIP subscription expires in the XMPP direction, the gateway must either cancel the XMPP subscription (treating it as temporary) or maintain it and send an unavailable presence notification.
sections.eli5: SIP subscriptions are like a library card that expires after a year; you need to renew it. XMPP subscriptions are like being on someone's friend list; they stay unless you delete them. Gateways need to translate between these two very different styles.

sections.title: Subscription Request Flow
sections.content:
When an XMPP user initiates a subscription to a SIP user, the flow is:

XMPP to SIP: The XMPP server receives the subscription request (a presence stanza of type "subscribe") and routes it to a gateway if the target is a SIP domain. The gateway translates it to a SIP SUBSCRIBE request with an Expires header. The SIP server delivers this to the target user. If the user accepts, the SIP server sends a 200 OK response and a NOTIFY message with presence data. The gateway translates the NOTIFY into an XMPP presence stanza of type "subscribed", and sends actual presence updates back to the XMPP user.

SIP to XMPP: A SIP user sends a SUBSCRIBE request to an XMPP target. The SIP server routes it to a gateway if the target domain is XMPP. The gateway translates it to an XMPP subscription request (a presence stanza of type "subscribe"). The XMPP user's server delivers this to the user. If the user approves, the server returns a "subscribed" stanza, which the gateway translates to a SIP 200 OK response. The XMPP server then sends presence notifications to the gateway, which the gateway translates to SIP NOTIFY messages.
sections.eli5: When someone from one system wants to follow someone in the other system, the gateway translates the "subscribe me" message. When the target person is available, the gateway translates "I'm online" back to the original system.

sections.title: Presence Updates and Mapping
sections.content:
Both SIP and XMPP can send presence notifications that update availability status. XMPP presence stanzas with no 'type' attribute mean the user is available; a 'type' attribute with value "unavailable" means offline. Optional elements like <show/> (away, do not disturb, etc.) and <status/> (a text message) add detail.

SIP presence uses NOTIFY messages with a PIDF (Presence Information Data Format) XML body. The PIDF <basic/> element is either "open" (available) or "closed" (unavailable). PIDF can also include optional extensions for extended presence information.

The RFC defines detailed mappings between XMPP and PIDF elements. For example: XMPP 'type' without value maps to PIDF basic status "open"; XMPP 'type="unavailable"' maps to PIDF basic status "closed". XMPP <show/> elements (away, dnd) can be included as PIDF extensions using the 'jabber:client' namespace. One-to-one mappings exist for addressing, request IDs, and other metadata.
sections.eli5: One system says "I'm online and away" while the other says "my status is closed but also send the away marker." The gateway uses a lookup table to convert each piece of information from one system's format to the other's.

sections.title: Subscription Lifecycle and Cancellation
sections.content:
An XMPP user can unsubscribe by sending a presence stanza of type "unsubscribe". The gateway translates this to a SIP SUBSCRIBE request with Expires header set to zero, which cancels the subscription on the SIP side.

A SIP user can cancel a subscription by sending a SUBSCRIBE request with Expires set to zero. The gateway handles this by either (1) immediately sending an XMPP unsubscribe, treating the subscription as temporary, or (2) maintaining a long-lived XMPP subscription and sending an unavailable presence notification followed by a zero-expiration SUBSCRIBE to the SIP user. The choice is implementation-specific.

When a SIP subscription expires naturally (the client does not refresh it), the gateway similarly has two options: cancel the XMPP subscription or treat it as long-lived and send unavailable presence.

The gateway also monitors subscription health. For example, if an XMPP-to-SIP gateway receives a SIP error response indicating that the subscription cannot succeed (403 Forbidden, 489 Bad Event, 603 Decline), it must inform the XMPP user by cancelling the XMPP subscription. Transient errors (423 Interval Too Brief, 481 Call/Subscription Does Not Exist) should be treated as temporary and the subscription preserved.
sections.eli5: When you unfollow someone, the gateway stops checking their status. When a subscription expires (like a library card), the gateway decides whether to keep asking their system or give up.

sections.title: Address Translation and Requests
sections.content:
Both XMPP and SIP use URIs to address users, but with different formats: user@example.com for XMPP and sip:user@example.com or sips:user@example.com for SIP. Gateways determine the target domain and route requests appropriately.

Both protocols support direct requests for presence information. In XMPP, this is a presence probe (a presence stanza of type "probe"). In SIP, it is a SUBSCRIBE request with Expires set to zero, which causes an immediate NOTIFY and then terminates the subscription. A gateway translates a presence probe into a zero-expiration SIP SUBSCRIBE, and vice versa.
sections.eli5: Each system has its own way of writing addresses and asking "are you online right now?". The gateway translates between them.
